paper_title: Target-Part Preference Optimization for Part-Aware 3D Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Part-aware 3D generation requires not only globally plausible objects but also complete, well-separated semantic parts, yet high-quality part decompositions remain too scarce to support large-scale supervised fine-tuning. We study whether preference fine-tuning based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) can adapt a pretrained part-aware generator from limited part-annotated data without architectural changes. We rank candidates generated with different random seeds against ground-truth (GT) geometric metrics, and select the (object, target-part) examples with the largest across-seed quality gap. Each selected example stores a seed pair whose two flow trajectories share one clean GT compositional latent and differ only in Gaussian noise. We derive a reference-relative target-block preference loss from FlowDPO that compares the two trajectories against a frozen reference model. GT flow-matching losses on the target block and complete part set provide absolute supervision, while only the diffusion transformer (DiT) is updated. Human-ranked controls test an alternative ordering source, and synthetic cropping provides controlled loser targets that are incomplete by construction. Among the three training-set scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest result on held-out Objaverse and outperforms both the pretrained generator and the reported direct supervised fine-tuning baseline on the multi-part aggregate. Further analysis shows sensitivity to pair ordering, target-part coverage, and the balance between pairwise and GT supervision. Cross-dataset experiments show less consistent gains under distribution shift.

Introduction Imageand text-conditioned 3D generators can now synthesize objects with convincing global geometry [22, 19, 8]. Many applications, however, manipulate objects at the part level. Editing component, recomposing an object, or articulating joint requires the relevant semantic parts to be complete, well separated, and independently usable [2, 14, 16, 18]. plausible overall shape does not guarantee these properties. Generated parts may still be missing, fused, or fragmented. Such local failures may be obscured by object-level evaluation but remain important for downstream use, motivating supervision that explicitly targets part quality. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on complete part decompositions is direct solution, but fine-grained 3D part annotations are costly and remain limited [21, 28]. Making effective use of limited number of annotated objects is therefore important. Preference optimization provides complementary source of supervision. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from ordered comparisons relative to frozen reference model without training separate reward model [23]. Diffusion-DPO and FlowDPO extend this formulation to diffusion and flow-matching generators by replacing likelihood ratios with denoisingor flow-matching-error surrogates [27, 9]. We ask whether preference-guided fine-tuning can adapt pretrained partaware generator from limited annotated data without degrading its object-level generation ability. Applying DPO to part-aware 3D generation is not straightforward. Existing 3D preference methods rank complete assets or rendered views [30, 12], while Mesh-RFT localizes feedback through quality-aware face masking [17]. These formulations do not directly address comparisons on one semantic part block in generator that jointly models several parts. Existing part datasets likewise provide decompositions, not ordered target-part preferences [21, 28]. This leaves two practical questions: how to construct reliable target-part pairs from limited annotations, and how to improve the selected part without degrading the overall object quality. We customize FlowDPO for target-part preference learning and fine-tune only PartCrafters diffusion transformer (DiT) without architectural changes [14, 9]. PartCrafter represents each part with separate latent-token block, allowing the pairwise error to be evaluated on selected target block. Among the tested scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest held-out Objaverse multi-part result, raising matched-part F-score by approximately 5% over pretrained PartCrafter and exceeding the reported direct-SFT baseline. We make three contributions. We devise GT-referenced ranking procedure that converts generated candidates into winnerloser seed pairs with varying seed-conditioned trajectories. We derive target-block preference objective from FlowDPO [9] and combine it with target-part and allpart GT flow-matching losses. We construct metric-ranked target-part training sets at three scales from PartObjaverse-Tiny [28], together with human-ranked and synthetic-crop controls. We analyze training-set scale, target-part coverage, ordering reliability, loser construction, objective components, and cross-dataset transfer to identify when target-part preference learning helps and where its gains do not transfer. 2. Related Work 2.1. 3D And Part-Aware Generation Modern 3D generation includes score-distillation methods guided by pretrained image models [22, 13], sparseview reconstruction [19], and feed-forward generators that predict 3D representations directly from images [8, 11]. These approaches substantially improve object-level fidelity, but plausible object surface does not by itself provide explicit, separately usable components. To generate better part components, part-aware methods generate or recover component-level structure through combining segmentation and reconstruction [2], compositional or contextual part latents [14, 6], autoregressive part discovery [3], semantic decoupling and structural cohesion [29], efficient multi-part packing [25], or retrieval-augmented generation and editing [10]. Explicit parts also support downstream articulation, where methods infer part graphs, joints, axes, or motion ranges [16, 18]. Our contribution is an alignment objective rather than new 3D representation. We evaluate this objective on PartCrafter [14]. 2.2. Preference Optimization For 3D Generation Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns model from preference pairs relative to fixed reference without training separate reward model [23]. Diffusion-DPO and FlowDPO extend this formulation to diffusion and flow models by replacing intractable output likelihoods with denoisingor flow-matching-error surrogates [27, 9]. Because such objectives depend on reliable preference labels, robust-DPO work also studies learning under noisy feedback [24]. Preference alignment has recently been applied to 3D generation. DreamDPO ranks paired renderings with reward-model or multimodal-model feedback during textto-3D optimization [30]. Circular-DPO transfers preference information across stages of 3D generation pipeline [12], while Mesh-RFT applies fine-grained reinforcement feedback to mesh generation [17]. DreamDPO and CircularDPO primarily rank complete objects or rendered views, whereas Mesh-RFT provides fine-grained mesh feedback. Our study instead compares reference-relative flow errors on one target-part latent block. Section 4.1 defines the metric-ranked construction and output-ranked controls. 3. Preliminaries

Method Our goal is to adapt the pretrained part generator from limited set of GT part decompositions so that it improves selected part while preserving the remaining parts. PartCrafter represents each part as separate latent-token block under shared DiT, allowing the FlowDPO error surrogate to be evaluated on target block p. This localizes the training signal, although the parameter update still affects the shared DiT. Three ingredients realize it: (1) preference pairs built offline by ranking seed-generated candidates with GT part metrics, so the winner and loser trajectories share one GT clean latent and differ only in seeded noise; (2) reference-relative loss on block that favors the winner trajectory; and (3) target-part and all-part reconstruction on the winner that supply absolute GT supervision and keep the surrounding object faithful. Sections 4.14.2 detail the pair construction and its controls, and Sec. 4.3 presents the objective. 4.1. We construct the main training set from PartObjaverse-Tiny [28]. After retaining objects with two to eight usable parts and removing parts whose face fraction is below 0.005, the set contains 140 objects and 796 target-part pair examples. For each example, the offline pair builder samples candidates and stores the winner/loser seeds, target-part index, and indexed GT geometry. During fine-tuning, the seeds generate independent noise for the same GT compositional latent, as defined in Sec. 4.1. Candidate-quality metrics are used only during offline pair construction and are not optimized as rewards. The automatic score is weighted sum of object FS/CD (0.35/0.20), target-part FS/CD (0.20/0.10), normal consistency (0.10), and component quality (0.05). Examples are ranked by the across-seed spread of this score on the indexed part. Supplementary Sec. S2 gives the complete definition. The training-set-size study spans three scales: small (56 realizations of the same GT latent. Optimization. First-stage checkpoints initialize from released PartCrafter weights, while the continued large-set checkpoint initializes from the preceding first-stage model. Fine-tuning updates only the PartCrafter DiT θ. The image encoder, VAE encoder and decoder, and stage-initial reference copy of the DiT remain frozen. The reported models use β = 0.10 and combine the reference-relative pairwise loss with target-part and all-part reconstruction. Matched reconstruction-only controls retain their corresponding training configurations but set λpair = 0. The primary control matches the medium-set first stage, and the secondary control matches the continued large-set setting. We use (λpair, λpart, λall) = (0.40, 0.30, 0.05), AdamW with learning rate 3 104, batch size eight, fp16, EMA, and classifier-free-guidance dropout 0.1 on single GPU. Supplementary Sec. S2 provides the complete settings. Evaluation Protocol. For each of the three source datasets, Objaverse [5], Amazon Berkeley Objects (ABO) [4], and ShapeNet [1], we construct one fixed evaluation list shared by all methods. Before evaluation, each list is filtered against the union of object identities used by all fine-tuning configurations. No training input image, GT mesh, or target-part annotation is therefore reused for scoring. Because PartObjaverse-Tiny is derived from Objaverse, the held-out Objaverse list is the closest to the training distribution. ABO and ShapeNet test transfer across changes in source provenance, category composition, and part statistics. Multi-part inputs are the primary evaluation because they require both component generation and part separation. Single-part inputs are included as an auxiliary case. Following PartCrafters evaluation protocol [14], we report L2 Chamfer Distance (CD) [7] and F-score (FS) [26] at the object level (Obj-CD/Obj-FS) and matched-part level (Part-CD/Part-FS). In this paper, target part denotes the part indexed by during training, whereas matched part denotes predicted part after assignment to GT part during evaluation. Across the main-paper tables, bold metric values improve on the corresponding pretrained result, and underlines mark the best fine-tuned setting for each metric. Part metrics sample 40,960 surface points per mesh, build GTby-prediction L2 CD cost matrix, and solve the rectangular one-to-one assignment exactly; an unmatched GT part takes penalty ρ = 1.25 max(1, max C) and FS = 0. Supplementary Sec. S2 defines point-cloud normalization, part assignment, and the FS threshold, which is set to 0.1 times the normalized reference bounding-box diagonal. 5.2. Limitations And Future Work Our gains are strongest on Objaverse and transfer less consistently to ABO and ShapeNet, whose category and decomposition statistics differ from PartObjaverse-Tiny. Broader pair collection across categories, part counts, thin structures, and target-domain samples may improve robustness. The method still requires part-level GT geometry as the reconstruction target, and offline pair ordering makes performance sensitive to candidate coverage, ordering reliability, and the selection criterion. Closing the loop by regenerating and rescoring candidates from the adapted model, while retaining smaller GT subset for reconstruction, is natural next step. Finally, because the preference loss acts on block but updates DiT shared by all blocks, stronger local alignment can shift whole-object geometry. Target-part and all-part GT flowmatching losses provide absolute supervision, while only the DiT is updated. Among the tested training-set scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest held-out Objaverse result, raising matched-part F-score by approximately 5% over pretrained PartCrafter and exceeding the reported direct-SFT baseline on the multi-part aggregate. Additional Related Work editing or articulation. This section expands the related-work context omitted from the main paper. It covers image-to-3D and text-to-3D generation, part-aware 3D generation, editable and articulated assets, and preference and reward alignment. Image-to-3D And Text-to-3D Generation. Recent 3D generation methods have made substantial progress in synthesizing object-level geometry from text, images, or sparse views. Score-distillation methods optimize 3D representations with guidance from pretrained two-dimensional (2D) diffusion models [20, 13], while sparse-view, feed-forward reconstruction, and large-scale shape-generation pipelines improve single-image or few-view reconstruction efficiency [18, 9, 11]. These methods provide strong object-level generation baselines, but their objectives do not by themselves guarantee that local semantic components are separated, geometrically complete, or directly editable. Part-Aware 3D Generation. Part-aware generation methods can be organized into several broad families. Decompose-then-reconstruct pipelines can segment multiview renderings, complete occluded part views, and reconstruct the resulting parts [2]. Native part-generation methods instead represent parts explicitly as latent or token groups, using compositional part latents, contextual part latents, or autoregressive part discovery [14, 6, 3]. Other work emphasizes semantic decoupling and structural cohesion [27], efficient multi-part packing [23], or retrieval-augmented part editing [10]. These works primarily improve the generator architecture, representation, or conditioning interface. We instead keep the pretrained PartCrafter backbone as the starting point and study an additional part-level training signal. Editable And Articulated Assets. related line studies whether generated parts are not only visible but also functional, editable, or usable in downstream asset pipelines. Articulated-generation methods infer part graphs, joints, axes, or motion ranges [15, 17]. Missing, fused, or geometrically weak parts provide unreliable structure for later Preference And Reward Alignment. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) compares ordered samples relative to frozen reference [21], and diffusion adaptations use denoising-space surrogates when output likelihoods are not tractable [25]. Noisy-feedback work motivates controlled order perturbations [22]. In 3D vision, CircularDPO transfers preferences across multi-stage 3D generation [12], DreamDPO ranks paired renderings with rewardmodel or multimodal-model feedback [28], and Mesh-RFT applies local face-level reinforcement feedback [16]. Our target-part loss evaluates one indexed PartCrafter Diffusion Transformer (DiT) latent block rather than semantic class label supplied to the generator. Each primary metricranked training example stores preference pair selected before fine-tuning. The two seeds create different Gaussian noise for the same ground-truth (GT) compositional latent. Candidate-quality information determines the offline pair order but is not optimized as an online reward. Humanranked controls replace automatic pair annotation with visual inspection of generated outputs. S2.
